why: Each subject costs max(0, needed[i] - answered[i]) extra questions to pass, and every pass is worth the same 1. To pass the most subjects with budget q, buy the cheapest ones first: sort costs and take them while the budget lasts.
hints: Turn each subject into one number: how many more questions it still needs.
Every passed subject counts 1 no matter its cost, so swapping an expensive pass for a cheaper one never hurts. Take the cheapest costs first.
Compute costs (clamped at 0), sort ascending, subtract from q until the next cost is larger than what is left. O(n log n).
pitfalls: If answered[i] >= needed[i], the cost is 0, not negative: such subjects pass for free.
Stop at the first cost you cannot afford; later costs are even bigger.
q can be up to 10^9 and the sum of costs larger; Python ints are fine.
statement:
A student is preparing for n certification subjects. For subject i, they have already answered answered[i] questions, and they need at least needed[i] answered questions to pass it.

The student can answer q more questions in total, split across the subjects however they like. Return the maximum number of subjects they can pass.

Worked example. answered = [24, 27, 0], needed = [51, 52, 100], q = 100.

  1. Extra questions each subject still needs: 51-24 = 27, 52-27 = 25, 100-0 = 100.
  2. Cheapest first: pass subject 2 for 25 (75 left), then subject 1 for 27 (48 left).
  3. Subject 3 needs 100 > 48, so stop. Answer: 2.

With q = 200 all three costs (25 + 27 + 100 = 152) fit, so the answer is 3. A subject where answered[i] >= needed[i] is already passed and costs nothing.
